\chapter{Evaluation}
\label{ch:results}

Chapter~\ref{ch:setup} fixed what was run: three models, seven scenarios,
three frameworks, one sample per task. This chapter asks what it shows.
Rather than walking through every task one at a time, it first validates
the load profile used to obtain every goodput measurement and then answers
five research questions that aggregate across every task, model, and
scenario collected. Model choice is a cross-cutting dimension rather than a
question of its own: each of the five is reported per model, so the
comparison between the three accumulates across the chapter instead of
sitting in one section. A closing summary draws the five answers together
and connects them back to the thesis's central
question (Section~\ref{sec:intro-missing}): \emph{can an LLM agent
iteratively optimise the deployment configuration of a backend application
on a Kubernetes cluster, guided by runtime performance feedback, to
maximise sustainable throughput under fixed infrastructure constraints?}

We achieved complete experiment coverage: all 63 of 63 tasks spanning
these scenarios, frameworks, and models were evaluated, and every task
reached a working baseline deployment and completed the full
ten-iteration refinement budget.


% ----- §5.1 Overview -----
\section{Overview of the Collected Data}
\label{sec:results-overview}

This section reports on \textbf{63 experiments} across the three models,
seven scenarios, and three frameworks introduced in
Chapter~\ref{ch:setup}. Each experiment records its per-iteration
goodput, the refinement lever applied, the resulting deployment-spec
knobs, and any failures observed; these records feed the figures and
summary statistics presented later in this chapter.

Every task in this chapter reflects a single run, generated from one
code-generation and deployment-generation seed
(Section~\ref{sec:setup-procedure}); Section~\ref{sec:methods-metrics}
gives the rationale for this design and what it does and does not
support. Goodput and gain,
introduced from Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1} onward, are positive,
multiplicative quantities and are summarised using geometric means.
Individual scenario-level points are shown alongside every aggregate so
the reader can assess variation directly rather than rely on a single
summary statistic. Section~\ref{sec:discussion-limitations} discusses in
more detail what this single-run design does and does not allow us to
claim.

\input{chapters/results_load_profile_validation}


% ----- §5.2 RQ1 -----
\section{RQ1: Does Iterative Refinement Improve Sustained Goodput, and How
Does That Differ Across Models?}
\label{sec:results-rq1}

\begin{table}[H]
  \centering
  \caption{First-non-zero-goodput vs.\ best-iteration goodput, by model,
    as geometric means over tasks with positive goodput ($n$ valid, out
    of 21). \emph{Healthy baseline} is the stricter count of tasks already
    serving traffic at iteration \texttt{000}. \emph{Gain} is the
    geometric mean of each task's own best/first-non-zero ratio.}
  \label{tab:results-rq1-summary}
  \footnotesize
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Model} & $n$ valid & Healthy baseline & First non-zero & Best & Gain \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} & 20 / 21          & 12 / 21          & 4{,}084           & 13{,}382          & $\mathbf{3.3\times}$ \\
    \texttt{gpt-5.5}         & \textbf{21 / 21} & \textbf{14 / 21} & \textbf{16{,}026} & \textbf{34{,}853} & $2.2\times$ \\
    \texttt{glm-5.2}         & 20 / 21          & 7 / 21           & 5{,}138           & 14{,}560          & $2.8\times$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/eval/baseline_vs_best_by_model.pdf}
  \caption{First-non-zero-goodput vs.\ best-refined-iteration goodput, per
    model. Boxes show the quartiles and full range across tasks with
    positive goodput; diamonds mark the geometric mean reported in the
    text and Table~\ref{tab:results-rq1-summary}; dots show every
    individual task (one scenario$\times$framework combination per model).}
  \label{fig:results-baseline-vs-best}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq1-summary} aggregates all 63 tasks by model,
comparing each task's first iteration with positive goodput against its
own best iteration and reporting the geometric-mean ratio between them as
the \emph{gain}. Figure~\ref{fig:results-baseline-vs-best} shows the same
comparison per model with every task plotted alongside that mean, and
Figure~\ref{fig:results-trajectories-grid} (further below) shows the 63
trajectories individually, one panel per scenario$\times$framework task.
Tasks that never record positive goodput at any iteration have no valid
gain reference and are excluded from these geometric means rather than
counted at $0$ (the table's ``$n$ valid'' column); the same two appear in
the trajectory grid as panels that never leave zero.

\texttt{gpt-5.5} leads on both ends, and not by a small margin: its
geometric-mean best is more than double \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s and
roughly $2.4\times$ \texttt{glm-5.2}'s, and it produces the most
already-healthy baselines (14 of 21), meaning it most often goes straight
into refinement rather than recovering from a dead start first.
\texttt{glm-5.2} sits at the other end of that measure, with half as many
healthy baselines, yet its geometric-mean best still edges above
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s: whatever state the baseline is in, refinement
closes most of the gap by the best iteration. \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}
shows the largest gain of the three ($3.3\times$) largely because it also
starts from the lowest first-non-zero goodput, so that figure says more
about where its trajectories start than about how strong its best
iteration is; Section~\ref{sec:results-rq5} traces the shortfall to a
pair of low-goodput \textsc{Rust-Actix} tasks that stall at their first
successful iteration, not to a general weakness of that framework for
this model.

Figure~\ref{fig:results-baseline-vs-best} adds what the table cannot
show. \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s first-non-zero geometric mean
($16{,}026$\,req/s) sits at or above both other models'
\emph{best}-iteration means: on average its baseline already reaches, and
slightly exceeds, the goodput level they attain only after refinement.
Nor is that an average pulled up by a handful of strong tasks, since its
whole first-non-zero box sits close to their best-iteration boxes and
even its lowest first-non-zero value ($1{,}883$\,req/s) exceeds either
model's lowest. The boxes also differ in width:
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} spreads widest on both sides, driven by the same
low outliers, while \texttt{glm-5.2}'s best-iteration box is the
narrowest, its refined tasks landing in a comparatively tight band
regardless of how healthy the baseline was.

\FloatBarrier
\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=1\linewidth]{figures/eval/goodput_trajectories_grid.pdf}
  \caption{Sustained goodput per iteration, one panel per
    scenario$\times$framework combination, coloured by model; note the
    independent $y$-axis per panel.}
  \label{fig:results-trajectories-grid}
\end{figure}
\FloatBarrier

\newpage
\paragraph{Refinement also rescues \emph{dead} baselines, almost always.}
Figure~\ref{fig:results-trajectories-grid} plots the sustained goodput
recorded at each refinement iteration, not the higher load levels
explore deliberately probes to find where the deployment collapses
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-load-profile}). A trajectory that stays at
$0$\,req/s therefore means the deployment failed one of the health gates
guarding refinement, the warm-up check, recovery, or the per-level
failure-rate check inside refine, not necessarily that it could serve no
requests at any load. Across all three models,
\textbf{30 of the 63 tasks} start with an unhealthy baseline, and
\textbf{28 of those 30} recover to a non-zero deployment somewhere in
their trajectory: all 7 of \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s dead baselines recover, 13
of \texttt{glm-5.2}'s 14 dead baselines recover, and 8 of
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s 9 dead baselines recover. Two tasks never
recover across the full ten-iteration budget: \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} and \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{TransitPulseDelayReporter}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}, the latter
recording exactly $0$\,req/s at every one of its ten iterations despite the
decision stage trying both code and deployment refinement across the
trajectory. The two fail for different reasons: the
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} application does become
healthy in its later iterations and explores to a transient peak, but never
holds a level through the recovery gate, so its \emph{sustained} goodput
stays at zero throughout; it is a genuine inability to sustain load, not a
deployment that never started. Refinement therefore contributes more than a tuning-speed
improvement: in most of these cases it brings a deployment that was not
clearing our health gate up to an accepted sustained-goodput level under
our load profile, though, as the two non-recovering cases show, recovery
is not guaranteed.

\paragraph{Improvement is not perfectly monotonic and can end in failure.}
Individual iterations often regress relative to the preceding successful
iteration, producing the sawtooth patterns in
Figure~\ref{fig:results-trajectories-grid}. Because the framework
updates the trajectory's latest \emph{successful}-benchmark reference
only after a completed run (Section~\ref{sec:methods-outcome}),
regressions are not silently
compounded: the next decision stage receives them as feedback, and most
trajectories recover within one or two iterations.
\textsc{BranchWeave}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} on \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}
is the sharpest exception. After reaching $25{,}327.3$\,req/s at
iteration~007, two consecutive deployment-refinement iterations, 009, which
reduced database replicas from 3 to 2, and 010, which reduced
\texttt{max\_connections} from 400 to 250, drove goodput to zero. The
trajectory then exhausted its budget, ending at $0$\,req/s despite having
reached $3\times$ its own baseline just one iteration earlier. Unlike the
dead baselines above, this task began healthy; it failed only at the end
of an otherwise successful trajectory, with no iterations remaining for
recovery. Section~\ref{sec:results-case-studies} discusses a milder case
that recovers more slowly but before the budget is exhausted.

\paragraph{Answer.}
\textbf{Yes, with two caveats.} Refinement improves sustained goodput in
every model whenever a task has data, and in a large majority of
dead-baseline tasks (28 of 30) it is not a marginal improvement but the
difference between a non-functional and a functional deployment. The
improvement is universal across the three models, but its shape is not:
\texttt{gpt-5.5} arrives at refinement with the most already-healthy
baselines and finishes highest in absolute goodput, \texttt{glm-5.2}
starts dead most often yet recovers from 13 of those 14 baselines to
finish narrowly above \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, and
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s leading multiplicative gain reflects its lower
starting point rather than a stronger endpoint. Which model is ``best''
therefore depends on whether the question is about the baseline call or
the loop that follows it. The size
of the multiplicative gain, however, is no fixed ``refinement value-add''
comparable across tasks: it tracks how under-provisioned the baseline
happened to be, most sharply on the near-stateless \textsc{ClickCount}
scenario, which makes it closer to a property of the baseline LLM call
than of the refinement loop. Separately, a fixed iteration budget is a
real risk and not merely a sample-size limitation: one task ends at zero
purely because its budget expired before it could recover from a late
regression.


% ----- RQ2 -----
\section{RQ2: Which Refinement Lever Contributes More: Code or Deployment?}
\label{sec:results-rq3}

\begin{table}[H]
  \centering
  \caption{Refinement steps chosen by the decision stage, by model and
    lever: how many failed outright (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6}) versus
    completed and reached a bench measurement.}
  \label{tab:results-rq3-funnel}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}l|rrr|rrr@{}}
    \toprule
    & \multicolumn{3}{|c|}{\textbf{Code}} & \multicolumn{3}{c@{}}{\textbf{Spec}} \\
    \textbf{Model} & chosen & failed & completed & chosen & failed & completed \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} & 111 & 3  & 108 & 99  & 5  & 94  \\
    \texttt{gpt-5.5}         & 107 & 15 & 92  & 103 & 0  & 103 \\
    \texttt{glm-5.2}         & 110 & 30 & 80  & 99  & 7  & 92  \\
    \midrule
    \textbf{All}             & 328 & 48 & 280 & 301 & 12 & 289 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Across all three models, the decision stage chose \textbf{code} refinement
328 times and \textbf{deployment (spec)} refinement 301 times.
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq3-funnel} breaks this down by model: $14.6\%$ of
the code choices failed outright before ever reaching a bench measurement
(non-compiling code, failing functional tests, and the other kinds
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6} catalogues in detail), against $4.0\%$ of
the spec choices. That gap is not uniform across models. For
\texttt{glm-5.2}, code refinement fails outright more than a quarter of
the time, by far the highest rate in this table and driven almost
entirely by the \textsc{Rust-Actix} compile failures
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6} documents, while its own deployment refinement fails
only $7.1\%$ of the time. \texttt{gpt-5.5} shows the same direction at a
smaller scale, with no spec failures at all, and \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}
is the one model whose two levers fail at comparable, low rates. For every
model, code refinement is the riskier choice in the narrow sense of
\emph{failing outright}; whether it still pays off once it does complete
is addressed below.

\begin{table}[H]
  \centering
  \caption{Of the completed steps in Table~\ref{tab:results-rq3-funnel},
    how many crossed the zero-goodput boundary in either direction, versus
    how many compare two non-zero measurements (\emph{clean}, the
    population Table~\ref{tab:results-rq3-summary} summarises).}
  \label{tab:results-rq3-boundary}
  \small
  \resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
  \begin{tabular}{@{}l|rrrr|rrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    & \multicolumn{4}{|c|}{\textbf{Code}} & \multicolumn{4}{c@{}}{\textbf{Spec}} \\
    \textbf{Model} & recov. & dead & collapse & clean & recov. & dead & collapse & clean \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} & 18 & 22 & 7 & 61  & 3  & 11 & 9  & 71 \\
    \texttt{gpt-5.5}         & 10 & 11 & 3 & 68  & 4  & 5  & 6  & 88 \\
    \texttt{glm-5.2}         & 21 & 15 & 9 & 35  & 11 & 15 & 14 & 52 \\
    \midrule
    \textbf{All}             & 49 & 48 & 19 & 164 & 18 & 31 & 29 & 211 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}%
  }
\end{table}

Of the completed steps, not every one compares two non-zero measurements
either. Table~\ref{tab:results-rq3-boundary} splits them further: a step
whose \emph{predecessor} already had zero goodput either \emph{recovers}
it (the successor is positive) or leaves it \emph{dead} (stays at zero),
and a step whose predecessor was positive either \emph{collapses} it to
zero or leaves both measurements comparable (\emph{clean}). Pooled, code
refinement recovers a dead predecessor about as often as it leaves one
dead, and collapses a working one comparatively rarely (19 of 280
completed steps). Deployment refinement shows the opposite balance: it
recovers a dead predecessor only about half as often as it fails to, and
collapses a working deployment proportionally more often than code
refinement does. \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s code refinement is the one partial
exception to the pooled pattern, failing to revive a dead predecessor
more often than it succeeds.

Neither a recovery nor a collapse can be pooled into a single
percentage-based average on equal terms: a $0$-goodput predecessor makes
the ratio undefined (a recovery cannot be expressed as a percentage at
all), while a $0$-goodput successor is always exactly $-100\%$ (a collapse
always can be). Averaging the two together would therefore count every
collapse but silently drop every recovery, which is why they are reported
here as counts instead.

\begin{table}[H]
  \centering
  \caption{Per-step goodput change (\%) by refinement lever and model,
    restricted to the \emph{clean} steps of Table~\ref{tab:results-rq3-boundary}
    (both predecessor and successor non-zero). Bold marks the best
    median/mean in each of the four value columns.}
  \label{tab:results-rq3-summary}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}l|rrr|rrr@{}}
    \toprule
    & \multicolumn{3}{|c|}{\textbf{Code}} & \multicolumn{3}{c@{}}{\textbf{Spec}} \\
    \textbf{Model} & $n$ & median & mean & $n$ & median & mean \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} & 61  & $+2.0\%$           & $+17.5\%$          & 71  & $\mathbf{+4.0\%}$ & $\mathbf{+16.4\%}$ \\
    \texttt{gpt-5.5}         & 68  & $+5.3\%$           & $+31.5\%$          & 88  & $+1.6\%$          & $+7.2\%$ \\
    \texttt{glm-5.2}         & 35  & $\mathbf{+11.2\%}$ & $\mathbf{+56.2\%}$ & 52  & $+1.5\%$          & $+10.9\%$ \\
    \midrule
    \textbf{All}             & 164 & $+3.9\%$ & $+31.5\%$ & 211 & $+2.6\%$ & $+11.2\%$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/eval/code_vs_spec_delta.pdf}
  \caption{Per-step goodput change (\%) relative to the previous
    \emph{successful} iteration, split by refinement lever and model,
    restricted to the same clean population as
    Table~\ref{tab:results-rq3-summary}. Steps that recovered from or
    collapsed to zero goodput are excluded here (Table~\ref{tab:results-rq3-boundary})
    rather than shown as an unmatched $-100\%$ floor.}
  \label{fig:results-code-vs-spec}
\end{figure}

For the remaining \textbf{164 code} and \textbf{211 spec} steps,
both measurements are non-zero and a percentage change is well defined.
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq3-summary} and
Figure~\ref{fig:results-code-vs-spec} compare this \emph{clean} population
by model and lever.\footnote{These per-step changes are summarised with
the arithmetic mean and median, not the geometric mean used for goodput
and gain elsewhere in this chapter (Section~\ref{sec:results-overview}): a
per-step percentage change can be negative, so the values are not
strictly positive and their geometric mean is undefined.}

\paragraph{Code refinement has a heavier tail and leads on mean for every
model.} Restricted to the clean population, the typical (median) step is
still modest for both levers (code $+3.9\%$, spec $+2.6\%$), but the code
\emph{mean} is pulled well above its own median by a handful of large
single-step jumps, up to $+705.7\%$ (\texttt{gpt-5.5}), $+630.2\%$
(\texttt{glm-5.2}), and $+259.5\%$ (\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}), where a
code change fixed a latent correctness or connection-handling bug that no
amount of replica or resource tuning could have addressed. Code
refinement's mean exceeds deployment refinement's for every model:
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} ($+17.5\%$ vs.\ $+16.4\%$, closely),
\texttt{gpt-5.5} ($+31.5\%$ vs.\ $+7.2\%$), and \texttt{glm-5.2} ($+56.2\%$
vs.\ $+10.9\%$), with \texttt{glm-5.2}'s code mean the highest of the
three despite resting on the smallest sample ($n=35$), a sign its figure
is carried by a few outliers rather than a broadly higher typical step.
Figure~\ref{fig:results-code-vs-spec} shows why: for every model, code's
points cluster near zero with a handful of individual steps clearly
separated above the rest, the same large jumps listed above, whereas
deployment refinement's points are more continuously spread and never
reach nearly as high, its largest single value across all three models
($+226.0\%$, \texttt{glm-5.2}) still sitting below code's
\emph{third}-largest value alone ($+288.9\%$). It is that small set of
isolated code outliers, not a broadly higher typical step, that decides
the code-mean ranking.

\paragraph{Answer.}
\textbf{Code refinement fails outright more often than deployment
refinement (14.6\% vs.\ 4.0\% of chosen steps, pooled), but once a step
completes and both its predecessor and successor are non-zero, code
refinement's mean exceeds deployment refinement's for every model.} The
two levers therefore trade gain against risk in opposite directions,
which supports keeping them mutually exclusive per iteration
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow}): code refinement carries the larger
increases because a meaningful share of them untangle a
correctness-adjacent bottleneck, the same class of bug BaxBench's
load-free evaluation cannot observe (Section~\ref{sec:rw-benchmarks}).
Deployment refinement is smaller on both median and mean and fails
outright far less often, but it is not risk-free once it runs: every
model has deployment-refinement steps that collapse a working deployment to zero.


% ----- RQ3 -----
\section{RQ3: Does Task Complexity Explain Which Scenarios Are Harder to Optimise?}
\label{sec:results-rq4}

\begin{table}[H]
  \centering
  \caption{Per-scenario difficulty signals, pooled over each scenario's
    nine tasks (three models $\times$ three frameworks). Endpoints and
    functional tests (FTs) are the static counts of
    Table~\ref{tab:appendix-scenarios}. Failures are all recorded
    iteration-level failures for that scenario
    (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6}); zero-end is the number of tasks whose
    final iteration reports zero goodput; median gain is the median
    best-over-first-positive-goodput ratio ($n=8$ for the two scenarios
    with a task that never records positive goodput, $n=9$ otherwise).}
  \label{tab:results-rq4-scenario}
  \small
  \resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Scenario} & \textbf{Endpoints} & \textbf{FTs} & \textbf{Healthy /9} & \textbf{Failures} & \textbf{Zero-end} & \textbf{Median gain} \\
    \midrule
    \textsc{ClickCount}    & 2 & 1 & 3 & 7  & 1 & $8.02\times$ \\
    \textsc{Recipes}       & 5 & 1 & 6 & 5  & 1 & $3.32\times$ \\
    \textsc{BranchWeave}   & 5 & 5 & 7 & 16 & 4 & $1.69\times$ \\
    \textsc{Petstore}      & 8 & 3 & 2 & 14 & 0 & $1.06\times$ \\
    \textsc{ParcelPinLockerPickup} & 6 & 4 & 5 & 7 & 3 & $1.84\times$ \\
    \textsc{SplitNestSharedExpenseLedger} & 6 & 4 & 6 & 7 & 1 & $2.04\times$ \\
    \textsc{TransitPulseDelayReporter}    & 5 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 1 & $3.41\times$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}%
  }
\end{table}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Every scenario receives the same nine tasks (three models $\times$ three
frameworks; Chapter~\ref{ch:setup}), so model and framework are held
constant across any scenario-to-scenario comparison and a difference in
difficulty is attributable to the scenario itself.
Section~\ref{sec:setup-scenarios} and
Table~\ref{tab:appendix-scenarios} record each scenario's static
complexity, its endpoint and functional-test counts. This section asks
whether that static complexity predicts three empirical difficulty
signals: how often the baseline already starts healthy, how often an
iteration fails outright (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6}), and how much
headroom refinement finds once something works (the
best-over-first-positive gain used elsewhere in this chapter).
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq4-scenario} reports all three alongside the
static counts.

\paragraph{Endpoint count alone does not predict difficulty.}
\textsc{Petstore} has both the largest surface (8 endpoints, 13
operations) and the fewest healthy baselines out of the box (2 of 9), so
more surface plausibly does give the agent more chances to get something
wrong on the first attempt. But \textsc{ClickCount}, the smallest surface
in the dataset at 2 endpoints, still starts dead in 6 of its 9 tasks, a
higher rate than several scenarios with two or three times its
endpoint count; a trivial API is not automatically an easy one to get
right on the first try. The two scenarios also diverge sharply on the
other end of a trajectory: \textsc{Petstore}'s tasks, once they do reach
a working state, have the least headroom left for refinement to find
(median $1.06\times$, barely above baseline), while \textsc{ClickCount}'s
have by far the most ($8.02\times$), and \textsc{ClickCount} is also the
scenario that produces the single largest best-over-first-positive gain in
the whole dataset ($66.7\times$). A naive two-endpoint
implementation, once healthy, is often far from its own ceiling; a
naive eight-endpoint one, once healthy, tends to already be close to it.

\paragraph{Failure kind, not just failure count, separates the two hardest scenarios.}
\textsc{BranchWeave} and \textsc{Petstore} have the two highest failure
counts (16 and 14), but for different reasons, and their composition
matters more than the raw totals. Some of this is definitional:
\textsc{BranchWeave} also has the most functional tests of the seven (5,
against 1--4 for the rest), so it mechanically has more ways to be marked
\texttt{functional\_test}-failed, and indeed 11 of its 16 failures
(69\%) are exactly that single kind, concentrated in the graph-shaped,
stateful playthrough logic the scenario exercises
(Section~\ref{sec:setup-scenarios}). \textsc{BranchWeave} also carries the
most tasks that end the iteration budget at zero goodput after starting
healthy (3 of 9), the pathological late-regression behaviour
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1} traces to specific \textsc{Rust-Actix}
tasks. \textsc{Petstore}'s failures, by contrast, spread across five of
the seven recorded failure kinds (\texttt{functional\_test},
\texttt{docker\_build}, \texttt{llm\_parse}, \texttt{timeout},
\texttt{unknown}), with no kind reaching more than half, and none of its
tasks end at zero. That pattern reads as
broad-based fragility from a large, multi-resource API surface rather
than one specific logic class going wrong, whereas \textsc{BranchWeave}'s
difficulty is narrower and traces to one identifiable behavioural class.

\paragraph{Answer.}
\textbf{Task complexity by endpoint count alone does not explain which
scenarios are harder to optimise.} Static complexity correlates loosely
with how often a baseline starts healthy, not at all with how much
headroom refinement finds, and only partly (and partly by construction)
with how often iterations fail; functional-test depth and failure-kind
composition track difficulty better than raw surface size. Difficulty
itself splits into at least two independent axes that do not move
together: \textsc{Petstore} is hardest to start but leaves the least
behind, \textsc{BranchWeave} starts easily yet carries this dataset's
sharpest regression risk, and \textsc{ClickCount} is trivial to build yet
the most rewarding to refine. A single complexity number would
distinguish none of these.


% ----- RQ4 -----
\section{RQ4: Does Framework/Language Choice Affect Achievable Goodput?}
\label{sec:results-rq5}

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/eval/framework_comparison.pdf}
  \caption{Best goodput reached per framework (symlog $y$-axis), split by
    model. Each dot is one scenario task; the horizontal bar is the
    per-model geometric mean for that framework. Tasks with zero goodput
    throughout are excluded from the bar, not shown at $0$.}
  \label{fig:results-framework-comparison}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Figure~\ref{fig:results-framework-comparison} shows full seven-scenario
coverage on every framework for every model, with two exceptions that
never reach positive goodput (\texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{TransitPulseDelayReporter}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} and
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s \textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask},
both already excluded in Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}). All but two of
the nine per-model framework geometric means therefore rest on seven tasks,
those two on six.

\textsc{Go-net-http} reaches the highest geometric-mean goodput for
\emph{every} model, peaking at $57{,}379$\,req/s for \texttt{gpt-5.5}.
Below that, the ordering is not consistent: \textsc{Rust-Actix} places
second for \texttt{gpt-5.5} and \texttt{glm-5.2}, ahead of
\textsc{Python-Flask}, while for \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} the order
inverts and \textsc{Rust-Actix} falls to the lowest framework geometric
mean of any model in this dataset.

That inversion does not mean \textsc{Python-Flask} is genuinely the faster
framework here. It is driven mainly by two of \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
seven \textsc{Rust-Actix} tasks being exceptionally low, \textsc{Petstore}
at $287$\,req/s and \textsc{ClickCount} at $2{,}917$; the trajectory of
both tasks never improves past its first success
(\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} shows the same $1.0\times$
stall for \texttt{gpt-5.5} too, at a far higher absolute goodput of
$27{,}294$\,req/s). The other five \textsc{Rust-Actix} tasks are in the
same range as \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s other frameworks, and the
geometric mean is very sensitive to a couple of low values.

\paragraph{Answer.}
\textbf{Framework sets an achievable-goodput ceiling that refinement
operates within, not around, and \textsc{Go-net-http} sets the highest
ceiling for every model.} What is model-dependent is not which framework
is \emph{best} but which is \emph{worst}: \textsc{Python-Flask}'s
single-process WSGI ceiling under \texttt{gunicorn} limits
\texttt{gpt-5.5} and \texttt{glm-5.2}, whereas for
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} two \textsc{Rust-Actix} tasks that stall at
their first successful iteration pull that framework below
\textsc{Python-Flask}, without indicating a general weakness of it for
this model. That inversion is a property of the data rather than of the
statistic, though the choice of statistic decides whether it is visible
at all: a median would hide exactly the kind of collapse RQ5 is built to
surface.


% ----- RQ5 -----
\section{RQ5: Prominent Failure Sources}
\label{sec:results-rq6}

\begin{figure}[H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/eval/failure_taxonomy.pdf}
  \caption{Recorded \texttt{failure.json} occurrences by phase: one bar
    per model within each phase group, stacked and labelled by failure
    kind, across all 63 tasks. Bold numbers are per-bar totals; smaller
    numbers inside a segment are that kind's own count.}
  \label{fig:results-failure-taxonomy}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Figure~\ref{fig:results-failure-taxonomy} splits the \textbf{61} recorded
failures by phase, model, and kind: \textbf{47} occur in the
\texttt{02-code} phase, \textbf{10} in \texttt{04-deploy}, \textbf{3} in
\texttt{03-spec}, and \textbf{1} in \texttt{01-decision}, so code-refinement
failures alone outnumber every other phase combined. Within the code
phase, two kinds dominate: \textbf{31} are \texttt{functional\_test}
failures, split 3 / 13
/ 15 across \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} / \texttt{gpt-5.5} / \texttt{glm-5.2}
and present for every model, and \textbf{14} are \texttt{docker\_build}
failures, every one of them \textsc{Rust-Actix} code that fails to
compile, concentrated almost entirely in one model: 12
\texttt{glm-5.2}'s, 2 \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s, none
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s. Together, functional-test and docker-build
failures account for 45 of the 61 recorded failures (74\%), and both are
correctness problems the agent is directly responsible for rather than
artefacts of the deployment path.

Two deploy-phase failure kinds each recur across more than one iteration.
\textbf{4} \texttt{crashloop} failures span three \texttt{glm-5.2} tasks
across two scenarios:
three on \textsc{ParcelPinLockerPickup}, two consecutive deployment-refinement
iterations (002--003) on \textsc{Go-net-http} and one code-refinement iteration
(004) on \textsc{Rust-Actix}, and a fourth on
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} (deployment-refinement iteration
004). In all four, the diagnostic shows every
backend pod already scheduled and running, then repeatedly
\texttt{CrashLoopBackOff} across every worker node, an application-level
crash rather than a resource shortfall. \textbf{2} \texttt{timeout} failures
appear on \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} task (iterations 005--006,
both deployment refinement): pods reach \texttt{Running} but a majority never
pass their readiness probe within the wait window, so the rollout never
converges even though nothing crashes. Both are genuine deploy-phase
outcomes distinct from the resource-infeasibility case the next paragraph
describes.

A separate, genuinely recurring deploy-phase issue shows up for two
different models: a \texttt{docker tag failed: ... No such image} error,
recorded as kind \texttt{unknown}, on \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} task (iterations 005--006)
and \texttt{glm-5.2}'s \textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} task
(iterations 005--006). Both recover within a few iterations. Recurring
across two unrelated models and scenarios makes a harness-level
build/registry propagation race more likely than a model- or
scenario-specific cause, though this dataset cannot confirm that directly.

Static spec validation itself is worth recording as a positive result:
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s \textsc{TransitPulseDelayReporter}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}
task (iteration 001) shows it \emph{correctly} rejecting a proposal before
it was ever applied, pinning all three database replicas onto one worker
node whose combined resource request (38{,}000m CPU) exceeded that node's
allocatable budget ($\approx${}28{,}800m). A second instance of the same
check firing correctly appears on \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{TransitPulseDelayReporter}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} task
(iteration 002), again a database placement pinning $32{,}000$m CPU onto
one node. Neither of this dataset's deploy-phase failures (the crashloop
and timeout cases above) is a resource-infeasibility case this check would
have been expected to catch; on the two occasions a proposal actually was
infeasible, validation caught it both times.

The remaining kinds are small in count but each a distinct, genuine
signal: \textbf{3} \texttt{spec\_validation} failures (the two node-pinning
cases just described, plus \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} task) and \textbf{3}
decision- or code-refinement \texttt{llm\_parse} failures (all
\texttt{glm-5.2}: \textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} at baseline,
and \textsc{SplitNestSharedExpenseLedger} on both
\textsc{Go-net-http}\,(iteration 006) and \textsc{Rust-Actix}\,(iteration
010)).

\paragraph{Answer.}
\textbf{The dominant \emph{genuine} failure mode is upstream of
deployment}, in code correctness, where functional-test and docker-build
failures together account for 74\% of recorded failures. The
cluster-execution path is nearly, not entirely, failure-free: the
crashloop and timeout cases show that a proposal passing static
validation can still fail at apply time for reasons validation was never
designed to catch, offset by two documented cases where the same
validation correctly rejected an infeasible proposal before it was ever
applied. A separate gap lies in reporting rather than scheduling: a
trajectory can end at zero goodput without a single entry appearing here,
as RQ1's \textsc{BranchWeave}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} task does,
because every one of its iterations completed as a harness-level success.


% ----- §5.8 Case Studies -----
\section{Case Studies: What Individual Trajectories Reveal}
\label{sec:results-case-studies}

The failure counts of Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6} are built from
discrete, labelled events, and by construction they can only report what
was labelled. The first two cases below sit outside that count entirely,
on the same task, yet each changes what the aggregate picture means; the
third looks at a healthy trajectory instead, to show what a
deployment-refinement decision looks like when it does track the workload
correctly.

\paragraph{Case study: a connection-pooling bug invisible to
single-container evaluation.} \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} baseline reaches a completed
bench but records \textbf{0} sustained goodput: the adaptive profile's
warm-up step fails health checks and explore never starts. Postgres logs
from that run show the deployment producing 919 errors during the load
window, dominated by two error classes:
\texttt{\small unnamed prepared statement does not exist} and
\texttt{\small bind message supplies N parameters, but prepared statement
requires M}. This is the classic symptom of a Go SQL driver using
server-side prepared statements against PgBouncer in \texttt{transaction}
pooling mode, where a prepared statement created on one physical
connection is invisible on the next pooled connection a later query lands
on. This bug is invisible to \textsc{BaxBench}'s original single-container
functional tests (which use a direct, unpooled connection) and only
manifests once the generated code is deployed behind the pooler this
framework introduces. Iteration~001 (code refinement) does not fix it
(goodput remains 0); iteration~002 (code refinement again, chosen freely
by the decision stage given the iteration~001 failure feedback) does,
jumping to $21{,}542.3$\,req/s. This is direct evidence that iterative
\emph{code} refinement, not deployment refinement, is the correct lever for
an infra-interaction bug the model could not have anticipated at
generation time, and that it can take more than one attempt.

\paragraph{Case study: a plausible deployment decision that backfires.}
On the same task, iteration~003's decision stage reasons as follows
(quoted verbatim from its \texttt{decision.json}):\footnote{The log is
quoted as written at generation time, so the model's own figures here
(the $\sim$19{,}000\,req/s goodput and the connection and CPU readings)
are its original-network measurements; the goodput values in the
surrounding narrative are the internal-network re-measurements of the same
iterations that form this chapter's ground truth, which is why the two
differ slightly.}
\begin{quote}
\small
``The code is now well-optimized (0\% failures, 19K/s goodput) and the
bottleneck is purely infrastructure: Postgres hits 200/200 connections
with PgBouncer \texttt{cl\_waiting} reaching 311, and db-primary CPU
saturates at 16.7 cores. [...] We should add database replicas, enable a
read pooler, increase Postgres \texttt{max\_connections} and PgBouncer
\texttt{default\_pool\_size}, and potentially reduce over-provisioned
backend CPU to free cluster budget for more DB resources.''
\end{quote}
The reasoning is a coherent read of the previous iteration's diagnostics
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-bench}), and the resulting spec does exactly
what it describes: database replicas 1 $\to$ 3, \texttt{max\_connections}
200 $\to$ 300, backend CPU request 2000m $\to$ 500m. The resulting
deployment, however, regresses to \textbf{0} sustained goodput. The next
iteration (004, code) recovers to $34{,}854.6$\,req/s \emph{without}
reverting the topology change, so the regression is not explained by the
added replicas alone; most plausibly the simultaneous $4\times$ backend
CPU cut left the application under-provisioned for its own request
handling while the new DB topology was still stabilising. The task goes
on to alternate lever choices through the rest of its budget, peaking at
$44{,}850.9$\,req/s at iteration~007 before settling at $40{,}414.0$\,req/s
by iteration~010, itself not a monotonic climb: the first of two
consecutive code-refinement steps (iteration~008) gives back roughly a
fifth of the peak, the second (iteration~009) recovers about half of what
was lost, and the closing deployment-refinement step adds $20$\,req/s to that, leaving the
trajectory below its own peak. Unlike
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s \textsc{BranchWeave}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix}
task (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}), this trajectory has enough budget
left after its own backfire to recover before running out.
\textbf{Lesson for the framework, not just the model}: this iteration
changed three spec fields at once, which is consistent with the
single-lever-per-iteration design (Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow}) but
does not prevent \emph{multiple fields within one lever} from changing
simultaneously, which limits attribution within a deployment-refinement step the
same way mixing code and deployment changes would across steps. RQ2's finding
that \texttt{glm-5.2}'s deployment-refinement steps collapse a working
deployment to zero goodput more often than any other model/lever
combination in this dataset (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}) suggests this
is not a one-off either for this task or this model.

\paragraph{Case study: a spec trajectory that tracks a workload's scaling
shape.} \texttt{gpt-5.5} on \textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}
produces a large gain ($17.0\times$, baseline
$5{,}725.9$\,req/s to best $97{,}137.7$\,req/s), and its deployment-refinement
steps move in a consistent direction across the run rather than
oscillating:

\begin{table}[H]
  \centering
  \caption{Spec-knob trajectory for \texttt{gpt-5.5}, \textsc{ClickCount},
    \textsc{Go-net-http} (selected iterations).}
  \label{tab:results-case-clickcount}
  \footnotesize
  \begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    Iter.\ & Lever & Goodput (req/s) & Replicas & CPU req.\ & DB repl.\ & DB max\_conn \\
    \midrule
    000 & baseline & 5{,}725.9  & 48  & 1000m & 3 & 500 \\
    006 & code     & 96{,}363.2 & 48  & 1000m & 3 & 500 \\
    007 & spec     & 96{,}738.6 & 192 & 350m  & 1 & 300 \\
    008 & code     & 96{,}494.9 & 192 & 350m  & 1 & 300 \\
    009 & spec     & 96{,}435.7 & 320 & 250m  & 1 & 500 \\
    010 & code     & 97{,}137.7 & 320 & 250m  & 1 & 500 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

By iteration~006 a code-refinement step has already lifted goodput to near this
task's ceiling ($\sim$96{,}000\,req/s, among the highest in the dataset);
the deployment-refinement steps that follow hold it there while moving deployment knobs in
a workload-appropriate direction rather than driving a further climb.
Between iterations 006 and 010, the agent roughly \emph{sextuples}
replica count (48 $\to$ 320) while \emph{quartering} per-pod CPU request
(1000m $\to$ 250m), trading a few large pods for many small ones, and
drops database replicas from 3 to 1. For a scenario whose endpoints are a
near-stateless counter increment (Section~\ref{sec:setup-scenarios}),
this is the correct qualitative direction: per-request CPU cost is
negligible, so raw horizontal fan-out beats per-pod headroom, and the
extra Postgres read replicas the baseline provisioned were never
load-bearing. \texttt{glm-5.2} reaches almost exactly the same ceiling on
its own \textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} task
($96{,}281.8$\,req/s, and the single largest gain in this dataset at
$66.7\times$), but not by the same route: its replica count ends where it
started (50), it halves rather than quarters per-pod CPU
(1000m $\to$ 500m), and it never provisioned the database read replicas
that \texttt{gpt-5.5} dropped. Its deployment-refinement steps oscillate across the run
(50 $\to$ 25 $\to$ 50 $\to$ 20 $\to$ 50 replicas) instead of settling on a
direction, so the two models arrive at the same ceiling on the same task
by visibly different deployment settings. Spec prompts intentionally
omit recommended numeric ranges (Section~\ref{sec:methods-spec}), so this
directional movement is evidence that, on this trajectory, the agent is
reading load-test and utilisation feedback rather than falling back on
defaults; the backfire case above, \texttt{glm-5.2}'s oscillating path on
this same task, and RQ2's finding
that deployment-refinement steps collapse a working deployment to zero goodput
more often for \texttt{glm-5.2} than for any other model/lever combination
in this dataset (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}), are enough to show this
direction is not guaranteed by the mechanism itself, only that it is
possible.

\paragraph{Answer.}
\textbf{Individual trajectories surface what a count-based taxonomy
structurally cannot.} The first two cases make the same point from
opposite directions: code refinement fixes a bug the model could not have
anticipated at generation time, and a single well-reasoned deployment
decision undoes a healthy deployment because nothing constrains how many
spec fields one step may touch. Neither appears in
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6}'s counts, since both iterations complete as
harness-level successes recording zero goodput, the same blind spot RQ1's
\textsc{BranchWeave}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} task shows at trajectory
scale. The \textsc{ClickCount} case is the counterpoint: the same lever
instead tracks the workload's actual scaling shape. A second model
reaches the same ceiling on that task by an oscillating path, which shows
the mechanism is capable of this, not that it reliably does it.


% ----- §5.9 Summary -----
\section{Summary}
\label{sec:results-summary}
% Legacy label retained so older cross-references continue to resolve.
\label{sec:results-synthesis}

Across all three models and all 63 scenario/framework tasks:
%
\begin{itemize}
  \item the instrument behind every goodput figure above is stable enough
        to carry the comparisons drawn from it: re-measuring a fixed
        candidate moves the estimate by a median $2.9\%$, refine corrects
        both optimistic and prematurely low explore peaks, and every run
        terminates on its own criteria inside a bounded budget
        (Section~\ref{sec:results-load-profile-validation});
  \item iterative refinement improves sustained goodput in essentially
        every task, and separately rescues 28 of the 30 \emph{dead}
        baselines observed into a working deployment; one further task,
        healthy at baseline, climbs well above it and then loses
        everything again at the very end of its budget (RQ1);
  \item code refinement contributes the largest single-step gains for
        all three models and exceeds deployment refinement's mean for all
        three as well, dominated by fixes to bugs that only manifest under
        load and cluster topology, exactly the class BaxBench's original
        single-container evaluation cannot observe
        (Section~\ref{sec:rw-benchmarks}); deployment refinement is
        smaller on both median and mean for all three, and fails outright
        far less often than code refinement does, but collapses a working
        deployment to zero goodput more often once applied, most severely
        for \texttt{glm-5.2} (RQ2);
  \item \textbf{all three models complete every task}, so the meaningful
        comparison is achieved goodput against cost: \texttt{gpt-5.5}
        reaches the highest absolute goodput without costing
        proportionally more, while \texttt{glm-5.2} slightly exceeds
        \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s goodput at roughly a fifth of the cost
        (RQ1; Appendix~\ref{ch:appendix-additional-results});
  \item \textsc{Go-net-http} sets the highest achievable-goodput ceiling
        for all three models; which framework sets the \emph{lowest} is
        not universal (\textsc{Python-Flask} for \texttt{gpt-5.5} and
        \texttt{glm-5.2}, but \textsc{Rust-Actix} for
        \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}) (RQ4);
  \item individual trajectories (case studies) show deployment-spec
        decisions that move parameters in a workload-appropriate
        direction, but not every deployment-refinement decision improves the
        outcome, even when the stated rationale is sound, and in one case
        the downside is severe enough to end the trajectory (RQ1);
  \item nearly all \emph{genuine} attrition happens at the
        code-correctness gate the agent is responsible for; the
        cluster-execution path is nearly, not entirely, failure-free, with
        static spec validation twice rejecting a resource-infeasible
        proposal before it was ever applied, and the failure taxonomy
        itself has a blind spot for trajectories that end at zero goodput
        without a harness-level failure (RQ5).
\end{itemize}

These findings are discussed further, including limitations and threats
to validity, in Chapter~\ref{ch:discussion}, and answered directly against
the thesis's research question in Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion}.
